title: What drove the move toward mackerel?
theory: Food pressure and fish availability contributed to a lasting shift in fishing effort, alongside markets and prior river damage.
known: The current graph contains temperature analysis, export-based biological inference and a proposed adaptation sequence.
missing: Independent catch or effort records
Dated market, trade and river-obstruction evidence
Comparison with places under different food pressure
supportWouldLookLike: Effort changes track local food pressure and fish availability after accounting for trade and access.
challengeWouldLookLike: A similar shift predates the shock or follows trade incentives more closely than local food pressure.
researchSteps: Compare dated records across at least two locations or periods.
Identify whether exports reflect catch, demand, reporting or trade access.
Retain interacting causes and uncertainty; do not infer populations directly from exports.

title: Did exposure explain differing flood losses?
theory: Floodplain exposure helped determine damage; severe weather did not produce identical agricultural outcomes everywhere.
known: The graph separates qualitative rain, reported Windsor flood losses and Hobart’s harvest expectation.
missing: Actual harvest and damage records
High-ground versus low-ground comparisons
Comparable rainfall and river conditions
Original Hobart newspaper passage
supportWouldLookLike: Under comparable conditions, exposed farms suffered greater losses than less exposed farms.
challengeWouldLookLike: Loss patterns are better explained by rainfall, crop timing or other conditions than residence location.
researchSteps: Check comparable localities and crop calendars.
Distinguish forecast harvests from realized returns.
Treat volcanic attribution as a separate question.

title: What changed where you live in 1816?
theory: A local change in 1816 may connect to the wider systems in this thread; that connection needs evidence.
known: The graph contains some regional records, but local coverage remains incomplete.
missing: Dated 1816 records for your place
Local prior conditions and alternative explanations
Evidence that distinguishes a local connection from coincidental timing
supportWouldLookLike: Local 1816 records support a specific mechanism and its timing.
challengeWouldLookLike: Local records contradict the proposed mechanism or fit another explanation better.
researchSteps: Choose a town, district, watershed or community.
Inspect 1816 records of weather, harvests, prices, population, work, health, politics or culture.
Use earlier/later records as comparison only; keep proposed observations in 1816.

title: Whose explanation of the Barbados uprising survives comparison?
theory: Registration proposals may have shaped emancipation expectations, but the colonial report alone cannot establish their contribution to resistance.
known: Codd attributes motives; Leith forwards his report. These are not independent witnesses to participants’ intentions.
missing: Participant perspectives and Barbadian scholarship
Dated evidence of communication and planning
Existing coercive conditions and competing explanations
supportWouldLookLike: Independent evidence links particular expectations to organizers’ choices.
challengeWouldLookLike: Records support other motives or show the official explanation misrepresents participants.
researchSteps: Inspect sources beyond Codd’s source family.
Separate prior conditions, new proposals, communication, organization and military response.
Record geographic and temporal limits; do not add a climate explanation without evidence.

title: Did purchasing networks change who could obtain food?
theory: Trade access and coordination may help explain different food outcomes alongside crop losses.
known: A later review describes failed talks and private buying; a model study does not fully explain regional disparity.
missing: Original conference and procurement records
Actual delivery and distribution dates
Comparable prices, wages, reserves and household access
Local crop, pasture and pest records with dates; exposure may differ before policy effects are compared.
BPUN 6R370 originals; eligibility, earnings and household food access before and after home-work relief.
MCE 165, 30 December 1816, pp. 1421–1422; AEN Assistance 3/IV reply of 4 February 1817. Test relief eligibility by domicile and origin using individual cases.
1816 Appenzell wage and price records, comparable work specifications, material costs and employment; compare KB-015011 handwriting with transcription.
Compare Zollikofer second part pp. 208–210 with scan and Appenzell December 1816 council/embassy papers; trace permission, payment, shipment and household access separately.
supportWouldLookLike: Dated records connect purchasing access to supply reaching households.
challengeWouldLookLike: Purchases failed to arrive or local differences fit exposure, income or other conditions better.
researchSteps: Choose two localities and check comparability.
Inspect 1816 records and trace the purchase-to-delivery-to-access chain.
Keep 1817 outcomes contextual; record inconclusive searches and rivals.
Distinguish crop-specific exposure and animal damage from access and income; do not treat all localities as equally exposed.
